title: When everything feels urgent: sort it, then act

audience.who: corporate employees with a full queue of requests from several people
audience.knows: their own work and tools; has felt the overload but has no simple sorting method
audience.cares_about: getting the important things done without working late or letting colleagues down

outcome: Faced with a list of competing tasks, the viewer can place each one by impact and effort, pick the high-impact small jobs to do now, schedule the big ones, and decline or defer the rest with a clear sentence.
through_line: Urgency is a feeling, not a ranking: once each task is placed by impact and effort, the order of work decides itself and saying no or later becomes a reasoned choice.

arc_plan.what: One employee, Monday morning, a list of requests all marked urgent; doing them in arrival order is the trap the viewer recognises.
Two questions per task, impact and effort, turn the pile into an order.
arc_plan.source_anchor: request: topic ('sort the work by impact and effort')

arc_plan.what: Draw the two axes on one board and place the running example's tasks; name the four zones only after the tasks land in them.
arc_plan.source_anchor: request: topic and notes ('one board that fills')

arc_plan.what: Act per zone: high impact small first, high impact big planned into the calendar, low impact small batched or later, low impact big declined or parked.
arc_plan.source_anchor: request: topic ('do the high-impact small jobs first, plan the big ones')

arc_plan.what: Saying no or later: tie the answer to the priority, offer a time or a trade, not an apology.
arc_plan.source_anchor: request: topic ('say no or later to the rest')

arc_plan.what: A new request arrives on the same board; the viewer places it before the answer is shown.
Back to the opening list, now in order, with a short re-sort habit when new work arrives.
arc_plan.source_anchor: genre: teaching arc (payoff returns to the opening)

must_cover.what: Sort tasks by two questions: how much impact, how much effort
Do the high-impact, low-effort jobs first
Plan and schedule the high-impact, high-effort work rather than starting it in scraps
Say no or later to low-impact work, especially the effortful kind
Urgency and importance are different questions; an urgent feeling is not the same as high impact
Re-sort when new work arrives instead of reacting in arrival order

must_avoid: statistics or research figures without a source on the knowledge sheet
attributing sayings to famous people unless the sheet grounds them
opening with a dictionary-style explanation of terms or an agenda
example_posture: One running example the whole lesson returns to: a single office worker's own week of real-sounding requests (a report for their manager, a quick reply a client is waiting on, a deck refresh, a meeting invite with no clear purpose). No invented company figures.
visual_direction: One whiteboard that fills by additions as the reasoning is drawn: the task list, then two axes, then tasks placed as sticky-note-like marks, then the zones named and the actions written beside them. One new thing drawn at a time; the person appears briefly at the start and the check.
voice_note: A capable colleague talking a peer through their own Monday: calm, practical, a little wry about the urgent label, never lecturing.
open_questions: Topic mode with no source: arc segments are anchored to the request and the genre; facts come from the knowledge sheet once approved.
Whether to name the matrix after Eisenhower depends on what the knowledge sheet grounds.

inferred: must_cover 5-6 (to be grounded by the fact-finder)
